body: A woman in her sixties is four hours into a coach journey she takes twice a year, with her coat rolled up against the window and one earphone in. A song comes on that she has known since she was nine. She has the next line before it arrives, the way you do. And the next line is not the line. It is close — the same melody, the same singer even — but a word has been changed, and the word that has been changed is the one the whole verse turned on. She sits with that for about a mile. Then she decides she must have been remembering it wrong, and goes back to looking out of the window.
She was not remembering it wrong. But she has no way of establishing that, and neither has anybody else, because the only copy of that song within reach is the one now playing.

Every track on this band carries a permanent twelve-character identifier. It is assigned once, it never changes, and — this is the part that matters — it is not derived from the title, the artist or the filename, all of which are things somebody can edit.

The distinction between a name and an identifier is worth slowing down over, because most people have never had cause to make it. A name describes. An identifier points. A name is for humans, which means it has to be readable, which means it will be improved, shortened, capitalised differently, translated, and eventually reused for something else entirely. An identifier is for the machine, which means it can be ugly, and being ugly is precisely what protects it. Nobody is tempted to tidy up twelve meaningless characters. That is the entire trick: the thing that holds a song still is worth nothing to anyone as a name, and therefore nobody ever touches it.

The identifier is how the schedule refers to a song, how the play logs record it, and how its Scripture and its credits stay attached as it turns up on one frequency after another across the 121 on this dial.

Committing to that at the beginning costs more than it looks. A permanent identifier means nothing can be quietly tidied later — not a duplicate, not a mistake, not a track somebody now wishes had been catalogued differently. It means ingest is slower, because uniqueness has to be verified before anything can air rather than discovered afterwards. And it means the awkward records stay exactly where they are, with their history attached, instead of being merged out of existence by somebody doing housekeeping on a quiet afternoon. The uncomfortable principle underneath is simple enough: anything that can be quietly swapped will eventually be quietly swapped, if only by accident.

Almost nothing else in a listener’s day works that way. The ordinary experience of media now is that everything is provisional. An article is silently updated after you have quoted it. A recording is replaced by a remaster with a different mix. A film is reissued with a scene altered, and the version you grew up with is simply not available to compare. None of this is conspiracy; it is what happens when the cost of changing a thing everywhere at once falls to nothing. The quiet consequence is that we have lost the ability to say what something used to be.

The arrangement inside the band follows from the same idea. A track that appears on several frequencies is the same object in each, not a copy per station, so the play log is a record of what actually went out rather than of what somebody meant to send. And because the Scripture is attached to the identifier rather than to a title, a song cannot drift from the passage it claims — the link has nothing to drift along.
This is the difference between a catalogue and a folder of music. It is not a technical preference.

Be fair to the alternative, because managing music by name is what almost everybody does and it works surprisingly far. Names are readable, searchable, memorable, and they let a human being find a song by half-remembering it, which is how humans actually look for things. But two different songs share a title constantly. One song carries four titles across three countries. An artist re-records and the new one inherits the old one’s name. A file gets renamed on somebody’s laptop in a hurry, and every reference to it dies quietly and without any error message at all. Nothing announces this. It is discovered years later by somebody who cannot work out why a link goes nowhere.
A name is a description. An identifier is a promise.

On a Saturday night a man of thirty-one is at his kitchen table with a laptop and a mug going cold, checking the tracks for the morning, which is a job he took on three years ago because nobody else offered. He is not really listening. He is ticking. Then he stops, and plays one of them again, and then finds the sheet the words were printed from. The recording and the sheet do not say the same thing. One line has been softened; not into heresy, just into something that means rather less than it did, and the congregation has been singing it that way for about eighteen months. It is twenty to eleven. He sits there working out whether he is the sort of person who mentions this.
Nobody swapped anything. Two things were connected by a title, the title stayed the same, and what sat underneath it moved. That is not a rare failure. That is the ordinary behaviour of names.

It should be said plainly that this is an unlovely thing to build an argument on. Nobody was ever moved by an identifier. It has no meaning, it cannot be remembered, it will never appear in anybody’s testimony, and describing a band this way makes a ministry sound like a warehouse inventory system. There is a real cost in that. A page of twelve-character strings is the least devotional object imaginable, and anybody who came here for worship is entitled to find it cold.

But every trustworthy thing anybody has ever relied on is trustworthy because of parts nobody admires. No one has ever wept over a foundation, and there is no hymn about load-bearing walls, and yet the room where the singing happens is only standing because somebody was thorough about them years before anybody arrived. The identifier is that kind of work. Its whole purpose is to be boring, permanent and unremarked, so that the things people do care about — a passage, a credit, a promise about what a song stands on — have something under them that does not move.

So a SongID is not housekeeping that happens to have been done tidily. It is what turns a file into a fixed object, and a fixed object is the only kind of thing anyone can actually be held accountable for. Every claim made anywhere on this band about what a song rests on is checkable for exactly this reason, and would be worth very little without it.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not theory.

Four kinds of programming sit on this dial and it helps to know they are there before you start turning. Most of the band is music — praise and worship, contemporary, country, gospel, hymns and a good deal besides. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and explained and prayed through rather than sung. There is family programming, which is simply safe to have on in a room with children in it, whether or not every track names God out loud. And there are the international frequencies, hosted in their own languages rather than translated into them afterwards. Every track on all of them carries the same kind of identifier.

If you want somewhere to begin, begin at HM 305.40 — Torah Sings. It is the station where this argument stops being administrative and starts being doctrinal, because its catalogue is Torah-rooted worship: songs that are not decorated with the text but built out of it. On a station like that, a title quietly coming loose from its passage is not an inconvenience. It is the difference between singing Scripture and singing something that used to be Scripture. Sunrise Praise runs from six and Evening Worship from eight, and every track between them stays attached to what it stands on because the attachment was made to twelve characters nobody has any reason to edit.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest and press play — it is built deliberately for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. If you would like it closer to hand, add the page to your home screen and it opens like anything else on it. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band learns which frequencies people are genuinely reaching for, which is how the next one gets built.

So treat this as an invitation rather than a specification. You do not need to care about identifiers, and there is no reason you should — that is rather the point of them. Put HM 305.40 on this week while you are doing something else, and when a line lands on you, look under it. The passage will be there. It will be the same passage in a year, and in ten years, and the only reason you will never have to think about why is that somebody decided, once, that a song is not a name.
